title: From Banana Leaf Meals to Fibre Bags: 10 Ways to Use Every Part of the Banana Plant
excerpt: 1 Plant, 100 Uses explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. In many Indian homes, the banana plant is a familiar sight. People buy its fruit at local markets, and they use its leaves during festivals and family gatherings. But the plant has uses that go well beyond what most people see in their kitchens. Farmers and artisans have found ways to use parts usually left behind after harvest. Some have been part of Indian food traditions for generations, while others are helping turn farm waste into useful products. Here are a few ways the banana plant is used across India. 1. Ripe bananas make an easy snack Bananas are eaten across India as a snack or alongside breakfast. They are easy to carry and can be eaten without cooking once ripe. The fruit is also used to make products that last longer than fresh bananas. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana documents the processing of bananas into products such as juice and banana fig. Banana pulp can also be used in jams and other preparations. 2. Raw bananas are a kitchen staple Raw bananas are cooked in homes across India. They are added to curries and dry vegetable dishes and are used in fried snacks. In Kerala, raw bananas are used to make the much-loved banana chips. The Nendran variety is particularly popular for this purpose. Raw bananas can also be dried and milled into flour for use in different food products. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented ways to process bananas into products with a longer shelf life. Such methods can help reduce losses when fresh produce cannot be sold or consumed in time. 3. The banana flower is cooked as a vegetable The purple flower that hangs beneath a bunch of bananas is used in several regional cuisines. Once the outer bracts are removed, the small florets can be cleaned and cooked in curries and stir-fries. Banana flower dishes are found in parts of southern and eastern India. The flower can also be made into pickles. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana flower pickle as a value-added product. Preparing the flower takes time because the florets need to be cleaned individually. But in households where it is a familiar ingredient, this is normally part of cooking with the plant. 4. The tender inner stem is eaten The part commonly called the banana stem is actually a pseudostem made up of tightly packed leaf sheaths. At its centre is a tender core that is used in cooking. In southern Indian kitchens, the core is chopped and cooked as a vegetable. It is also used in juices and other preparations. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented products such as candy and pickles made from the central core. Using the inner core for food gives households another way to make use of the plant after its fruit has been harvested. 5. Banana leaves are used to serve food A meal served on a banana leaf is a familiar sight in many parts of southern India. The broad leaf holds rice and several accompaniments and is widely used during weddings and festivals. Banana leaves are also used to wrap certain foods and serve meals at community gatherings. Their size makes them convenient for serving a complete meal on one surface. The leaves have a place in traditional food practices as well as in everyday hospitality. Their use varies by region and occasion. 6. The pseudostem is turned into fibre After the banana bunch is harvested, the pseudostem is cut down. Instead of leaving all this material unused, farmers and entrepreneurs can process it to extract natural fibre. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research has documented banana fibre processing technology and its transfer to an entrepreneur in Uttar Pradesh. The fibre can be used to make ropes and garments as well as mats and carpets. Bags and baskets are other possible products. Processing the pseudostem requires equipment and suitable facilities. Where these are available, the material can become a source of raw material for small businesses. 7. Banana fibre is used in handicrafts The fibre extracted from banana plant material can be used to make items such as table mats and cushion covers. These products offer another use for material left behind after harvesting. In January 2024, the ICAR National Research Centre for Banana organised a training programme in Tamil Nadu on banana fibre craft and value addition. The programme aimed to help women learn skills that could be used to make products from banana sheath and its by-products. The ICAR report on the programme describes the initiative and its focus on developing craft skills. For those with access to training and buyers, such work can provide an additional source of income. 8. Banana peels need not go straight into the bin Banana peels are usually discarded once the fruit has been eaten. Yet they can be put to use in food processing and composting. The ICAR National Research Centre for Banana has documented banana peel pickle as one way of using this part of the fruit. At home, the peels can be chopped and added to a compost bin along with other kitchen scraps and dry material. As the organic matter breaks down, it becomes part of the compost. This is a practical option for households that grow plants or maintain a garden. 9. Banana plants are used during ceremonies Banana plants are commonly used to decorate entrances and ceremonial spaces during weddings and religious occasions in several parts of India. Their green leaves and upright pseudostems are a familiar part of these arrangements. The plant is associated with auspicious occasions in many communities. The exact customs differ across regions, but banana plants continue to feature in traditional celebrations. Their role during these occasions is distinct from their use as food or raw material. They are part of the way families mark important events. 10. Banana residue can be used on farms Harvesting bananas leaves behind considerable plant material. The pseudostem and other suitable residues can be considered for composting or other forms of farm use rather than being discarded without thought. Research published through the Indian Council of Agricultural Research discusses banana plant parts and their place in integrated farming systems. The best use depends on the farm and the resources available. Some growers may be able to supply material to fibre processors while others may find composting more practical. Making use of what remains The banana plant serves different purposes in different parts of India. Its fruit and flower are cooked in homes while its leaves are used for serving food. These uses also offer farmers and small businesses ways to get more value from a crop. With suitable processing and local demand, parts of the plant that are left behind can become useful materials.

After receiving information about a leopard sighting, officials […]Hyderabad : A man was arrested by Forest Department officials and Nagole police for circulating an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated fake image of a leopard in a residential area of Nagole, triggering panic among residents. The incident occurred in the Fatullaguda area near Bhashyam School, within Nagole limits. After receiving information about a leopard sighting, officials from the Uppal and Hayathnagar forest ranges rushed to the spot. Forest officials find no signs of leopard A field inquiry found no wild animal at the location. Officials subsequently discovered that a man had used ChatGPT to create a fake image showing a leopard and circulated it online. The image caused concern among local residents late at night. Accused handed over to Nagole police The accused was identified as Sachin, a native of Karnataka who currently works in catering services in Nagole. He was reportedly found to be under the influence of alcohol. His blood alcohol level was recorded at 87 mg, according to the press note, which did not specify the unit or testing details. Forest officials later handed him over to Nagole police. A criminal case was registered under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for allegedly creating public panic and obstructing the discharge of official duties. Forest Department urges public to verify information The Forest Department has appealed to the public not to create or circulate fake wildlife images or misinformation using artificial intelligence tools on social media. Officials warned that sharing unverified information could cause unnecessary panic and obstruct government officials in the discharge of their duties. ]]>

title: 25% of Gen Z use AI for gift ideas; food and fashion lead festive spending: Study
excerpt: New Delhi: Venture capital firm Rukam Capital, in collaboration with YouGov, has released a study titled Gen Z: A Deep Dive into India’s Most Influential Consumer Cohort, which looks at how young Indians use AI, online search and social media to discover gifts, and what they spend on during festivals. The survey, conducted among 4,002 respondents aged 18–29 across 18 states, found that 25% of respondents use artificial intelligence (AI) to suggest gift ideas. Online search was the most cited source of gift ideas, used by 41% of respondents, narrowly ahead of personal judgement at 39%. AI-assisted gift discovery was highest in Madhya Pradesh (32%) and Bihar (30%). Social media also influenced gift discovery, particularly in Bihar, where 37% of respondents relied on it for recommendations, followed by Kerala and Telangana at 31% each. Food and fashion dominate festive purchases The study found that food and fashion were the leading festive spending categories nationally, with 49% of respondents reporting purchases in each category. Gifting followed at 36%, traditional or religious items at 35%, and home décor at 33%. However, spending preferences varied across states. Fashion led festive purchases in Chhattisgarh, with 61% of respondents reporting spending in the category. In Bihar, food topped the list at 59%, followed by fashion at 51%. Punjab recorded strong spending on food (54%) and gifting (48%), while in Telangana 56% of respondents reported spending on food and 53% on fashion. In Delhi, traditional or religious items (43%) and gifting (42%) were prominent spending categories. Meanwhile, travel emerged as a notable festive spending preference in Kerala (31%) and Gujarat (29%). Dining out was also significant in Gujarat (28%) and West Bengal (33%). Gen Z spending rises during festivals The survey found that 60% of respondents increased their expenditure during major festivals, including 25% who spent significantly more and 35% who spent somewhat more. Delhi and Punjab recorded particularly high festive spending increases, with 65% of respondents in each market reporting higher expenditure, followed by Rajasthan at 63%. Festive purchases also combined planning with impulse buying. Nationally, 40% described their shopping as a mix of planned and spontaneous purchases, while 31% said they mostly planned their spending. Family expectations emerged as the leading reason for overspending, cited by 34% of respondents, followed by discounts (29%) and emotional connections (28%). The findings also showed that family members remained the primary recipients of festive gifts, with 74% of respondents buying gifts for parents or family members, followed by friends (61%) and partners (39%). The findings are based on survey responses rather than actual retail transaction data. State-level results reflect the surveyed Gen Z respondents and may not represent the entire population of each state.

title: Liechtenstein Prince arrives in Delhi, set to hold bilateral talks with PM Modi on Tuesday
excerpt: Liechtenstein's Hereditary Prince Alois arrived in New Delhi on Monday as part of his ongoing State Visit to India which aims at further strengthening bilateral ties. Prince Alois arrived in the national capital from Gujarat's Vadodara. He was received by Union Minister of State (MoS) Jayant Singh at the airport."A new chapter in India–Liechtenstein engagement. H.S.H. Hereditary Prince Alois of Liechtenstein arrived in New Delhi today, following his visit to Vadodara, as part of his ongoing State Visit to India. He was received by MoS Jayant Singh at the airport. The visit will provide renewed impetus to the bilateral relations," the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) posted on X.Extending a warm welcome to Prince Alois, MoS Singh took to X and posted: "Following our earlier engagement at Davos, I look forward to further strengthening the warm and friendly ties between India and Liechtenstein and advancing our shared interests through greater cooperation."Prince Alois arrived in Mumbai on Sunday as he began his State Visit at the invitation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He is accompanied by his wife, Princess Sofia, and a high-level official and business delegation comprising top industry leaders."A warm welcome to India! H.S.H. Hereditary Prince Alois of Liechtenstein arrived in Mumbai on a State Visit to India. He was received by Shri Jaykumar Rawal, Minister of Protocol, Government of Maharashtra. India–Liechtenstein share warm and cordial relations, based on shared values," the MEA posted on X.This is the second visit of Prince Alois to India in 2026, as he had earlier visited New Delhi in February to attend the AI Impact Summit. He had previously visited India in 2010 and 2018. Prince Alois will be accorded a ceremonial reception at Rashtrapati Bhavan on Tuesday. He will pay a tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat and have a meeting with External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar. Prince Alois is scheduled to hold talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Hyderabad House later on Tuesday, where they will discuss cooperation in various sectors, including trade and investment, science, technology and innovation, and people-to-people exchanges besides also views on regional and global developments. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Union Minister of State for Skills Development and Entrepreneurship Jayant Chaudhary will call on Prince Alois on Tuesday. Prince Alois will then meet President Droupadi Murmu, who will also host an official banquet in his honour."The visit is expected to provide further impetus to the growing engagement between India and Liechtenstein, particularly since the operationalisation of the India–EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement in 2025. The visit will provide an opportunity to further deepen the friendly ties between India and Liechtenstein and build partnerships in new areas of mutual interest," the MEA said in a statement.
